question_text:
The following text is from an original short story.

Night-shift pharmacist Ibrahim Sorel tells the new technician that after midnight every refill should go through the side window. "Shorter line, fewer interruptions," he says. Yet he never opens the window until the lobby is empty, and when Mrs. Vance counts out coins for her husband's pills, he angles the register screen toward himself, rings the total in a low voice, and slides the bag across with the receipt folded small. Twice he has dropped his pen while she counted. The technician has yet to see the line at that hour hold more than two people.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
answer_a: Sorel arranges the overnight routine so that customers who struggle to pay can do so unobserved.
answer_b: Sorel prefers the side window because it keeps lines short and prevents interruptions at night.
answer_c: The new technician is learning to distrust routines that seem more efficient than they truly are.
answer_d: Mrs. Vance's trouble paying has led Sorel to rethink how the pharmacy sets its prices.
explanation: Sorel gives efficiency as his reason, but his actions point elsewhere. He waits until the lobby is empty, angles the screen away from the counter, speaks quietly, folds the receipt small, and drops his pen while Mrs. Vance counts. The technician also has yet to see the line hold more than two people. Together these details suggest that the routine exists to spare customers who count coins from being watched, which is what choice A says.
distractor_b_explanation: This is the reason Sorel states aloud. The passage undercuts it: the line never holds more than two people, and most of his behavior has nothing to do with speed. It is a surface reading.
distractor_c_explanation: The technician does see that the stated reason does not fit, but the passage never says the technician is learning to distrust routines in general. The focus is Sorel's treatment of customers, not the technician's development.
distractor_d_explanation: Mrs. Vance's struggle is shown, but the passage says nothing about Sorel rethinking pricing. He changes how he treats customers, not what the pharmacy charges, so this goes beyond the text.

question_text:
The following text is from an original short story.

The address book came in a shoebox with my aunt's reading glasses. For two Decembers I left it in the hall closet and mailed cards only to people I already knew. The third year I took it out, copied the names into a spreadsheet, and deleted every entry that had no phone number. The list went from ninety-one names to forty. I printed forty labels and stacked the envelopes by the door. Then I took the book back out and, with her fountain pen, which still worked, addressed the other fifty-one by hand, in her order, beginning with the Abernathys. I finished near midnight.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
answer_a: The narrator goes from leaving an inherited address book unused to addressing cards to everyone in it.
answer_b: The narrator discovers that a spreadsheet makes an old holiday task much easier.
answer_c: The narrator puts off an inherited task for two years before finally cutting the list to those with phone numbers.
answer_d: The narrator concludes that a faster method is not worth using when a task has personal meaning.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because the narrator's actions, described without comment, show a change in how the narrator treats the address book. The narrator first leaves it in a closet for two Decembers and writes only to people already known, then cuts the list from ninety-one names to forty, and finally takes the book back out and addresses the remaining fifty-one names by hand, in the aunt's order and with her pen. This progression goes from leaving the book unused to addressing cards to everyone in it.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The narrator does use a spreadsheet, but the narrator ends up addressing fifty-one envelopes by hand anyway, so the text does not show the spreadsheet making the task easier.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It is true of the first part of the passage only. The narrator does put off the book and cut the list, but then addresses envelopes to every name in the book, so the passage does not end with a reduced list.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The narrator does switch to hand addressing at the end, but the narrator never states a conclusion about faster methods or personal meaning; this attributes a lesson the text does not give.

question_text:
The following text is from an original short story.

Nadia had run the print shop's big press for three weeks when she noticed that her finished jobs vanished from the delivery shelf each night. Pell, who had managed the shop for thirty years, never mentioned it. When she asked about the wedding programs, he grunted and kept his back to her while he swept. She began checking her registration marks twice, then three times, sure he thought her careless. On Friday she opened the ticket drawer to file a late order. Each earlier ticket carried her initials alone, though every job number appeared twice. Under them lay bundles of her original sheets, tied with string, each one smeared where the colors had slipped out of register.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
answer_a: A newcomer grows more skilled after learning to inspect her own work more carefully than she once did.
answer_b: A newcomer realizes that a coworker's silence has been a way of quietly redoing her flawed work.
answer_c: A veteran's refusal to praise a newcomer shows his resentment at being replaced by someone less experienced.
answer_d: A newcomer learns that the press she was assigned has a fault that has made her work look worse than it is.
explanation: Choice B is correct. Pell never explains why her jobs disappear, and Nadia first reads his silence as disapproval. The late details suggest otherwise: every job number appears twice, which strongly suggests each job was run again, and her original sheets, smeared where the colors slipped out of register, were kept rather than delivered. The tickets still carry only her initials. Together these details suggest that Pell has been quietly redoing her flawed work while she learns, so the text centers on her coming to see his behavior as protective rather than critical.
distractor_a_explanation: Nadia does begin checking her registration marks more often, but that is a minor detail and a reaction to her misreading of Pell. The text never says her skill improves, and the ending concerns what she finds in the drawer, not her technique.
distractor_c_explanation: Pell is gruff and silent, but nothing in the text suggests resentment or any fear of being replaced. The tickets listing only her initials and the kept sheets suggest protection, not bitterness.
distractor_d_explanation: The text never mentions a fault in the press or any reason to suspect one. The smeared sheets are presented as her original work, and what Nadia discovers is how Pell has handled that work, not a mechanical defect.

question_text:
The following text is from an original poem.

Every Saturday I oil the vise
on his side of the bench,
though his hands have moved on to bigger tools.
I wipe the shavings from his stool
and leave it pulled out an arm's width.
When the delivery man comes, I point
to the cabinet by the door,
its corners so tight a coin won't slip,
and say, My brother, before he asks.
Then I hang the apron on its hook
where the window light lands,
and sweep my own half slowly,
and then his again.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
answer_a: The speaker is mainly concerned with keeping the cabinet by the door in good condition for a delivery man.
answer_b: The speaker follows a Saturday routine that prepares the whole workshop for the next job to arrive.
answer_c: The speaker's upkeep of a brother's side of the bench conveys admiration for his work and a sense that he is missed.
answer_d: The speaker resents that a brother left the workshop and finds quiet satisfaction in sweeping up alone every week.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The speaker repeatedly tends the brother's half of the bench even though his "hands have moved on to bigger tools": oiling his vise, wiping his stool, leaving it pulled out, hanging his apron, and sweeping his side a second time. The speaker also volunteers "My brother" before the delivery man asks about the cabinet, pointing to its tight corners. The upkeep of an unused place suggests how much his absence is felt, and the quick credit suggests pride in his skill, so the poem conveys both feelings without ever naming them.
distractor_a_explanation: Incorrect. This choice fixes on one detail, the cabinet, and a visitor who appears only briefly. The speaker also oils the vise, wipes the stool, hangs the apron, and sweeps the brother's half twice, none of which concerns the delivery man. The choice also leaves out what the speaker feels about the brother.
distractor_b_explanation: Incorrect. This choice summarizes the routine as ordinary preparation for work, but the poem never mentions upcoming jobs. It also misses why the speaker keeps up a side whose owner's hands "have moved on to bigger tools." The poem is about what the routine suggests, not about readiness for work.
distractor_d_explanation: Incorrect. The text does not support resentment. The speaker volunteers "My brother" to the delivery man before being asked and lingers over the brother's side, which suggests admiration and longing, not bitterness. Nothing in the poem presents the sweeping as a satisfaction of being alone.
